Full text

Abstract

View-only link to data and analysis scripts: https://osf.io/mky3c/overview?view_only=06f4c3ae6cbd4f9ea8e1864a793aa3a3 Supplements can be provided upon request and will otherwise be published with the peerreviewed manuscript.

Introduction

Chronic pain is a highly prevalent (Calvo et al., 2025) as well as heterogeneous condition, requiring interdisciplinary and multimodal treatment approaches (Breivik et al., 2006; Cohen et al., 2021; Sundström et al., 2025; Turk, 1990). Among psychological treatments, cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) are recommended by multiple guidelines (Becker & Straßner, 2023; National Institute for Health and Care Excellence [NICE], 2021). However, treatment effects at the group level remain moderate (Vlaeyen & Crombez, 2020; Williams et al., 2020), and even seemed to become smaller with improving meta-analytic methods (McCracken, 2023). Given the heterogeneity of chronic pain syndromes and the substantial variability in individual treatment responses (McCracken & Turk, 2002; Scholten et al., 2025), it is plausible that nomothetic, group-based research might not adequately capture individual treatment effects (Gloster et al., 2024). This heterogeneity encompasses comorbidities (e.g., Desai et al., 2020), previous and ongoing treatments, functional limitations, and psychosocial circumstances ('Guiding Principles', 2023). At the same time, the availability of high-quality treatment and specialised clinicians is often limited and waiting time for a treatment can be from months to over a year, depending on the country of residence or region (e.g. Baker et al., 2024; Grant et al., 2023; Purcell et al., 2022). In line with a biopsychosocial understanding of chronic pain and to address these challenges, personalised treatment and research approaches targeting disabilitymaintaining processes targetable in therapy are increasingly advocated (Bartels et al., 2022; Finan & Garland, 2015; McCracken, 2023; Murillo et al., 2022; Scholten et al., 2025; Turk, 1990; Vlaeyen & Morley, 2005). These efforts require clear clinical recommendations to enable evidence-based personalised treatment.

Definition of terms

The terms "processes of change" and "mechanisms of change" are often used interchangeably. While mechanisms of change are commonly defined as mediating pathways that explain how an intervention leads to changes in outcomes (Ehring et al., 2022; Kazdin, 2007), Hayes and colleagues conceptualize processes of change more broadly as dynamic, potentially non-linear phenomena that may operate across multiple levels of analysis (Hayes et al., 2020). Furthermore, processes of change should be theory-based and modifiable.

However, while this framework specifies characteristics that processes should exhibit, it does not provide a clearly delineated set of processes themselves. In the present study, processes were derived from established psychological models of chronic pain (Scholten & Glombiewski, 2024), for example avoidance behaviour as described in the fear-avoidance model (Vlaeyen et al., 2016). Accordingly, the processes used in this study are theory-derived constructs that have been proposed to contribute to the maintenance of pain-related disability and other burdensome pain-related experiences. These processes are not assumed to represent isolated causal mechanisms but are used to derive clinically meaningful treatment targets for personalised intervention selection. Thus, we use the term process when referring to general psychological processes and their assessment, while the term treatment target denotes a specific process selected in the context of treatment and clinical decision-making. All treatment targets are therefore process-based.

More specifically, treatment targets represent clinically actionable manifestations of broader psychological processes, for example asking others to take over a strenuous task (target) as a specific manifestation of avoidance behaviour (process). The specific processes are listed in the Study Materials section and the individual targets are summarised in Table 2.

Following our previous definition (Reference), an intervention is embedded within a treatment module that provides structure to its implementation, including preparation, execution, and consolidation. A treatment module extends beyond the isolated delivery of an intervention. For example, exposure in vivo may involve preparatory elements that establish treatment rationale and commitment (e.g., creating a movement hierarchy), the intervention itself (e.g., behavioural exposure), and procedures intended to consolidate treatment effects (e.g., self-management goals).

To link treatment modules to predefined treatment targets in a transparent and reproducible manner, a Matching Matrix is required. A Matching Matrix therefore does not encompass the full clinical decision-making process and does not determine which treatment target should be prioritised. Rather, it supports the selection of a treatment module once a target has been identified. In contrast, an algorithm encompasses the broader clinical decisionmaking process, including both target selection and treatment module indication (Reference).

Personalisation strategies

In routine clinical practice, therapists already personalise treatment because recommendations derived from nomothetic averages frequently do not fit individual patients (Levinson et al., 2024). CBT therapists therefore rely on case conceptualisations and flexible adaptations of treatment protocols -an approach that calls the utility of protocols into question (McCracken, 2023). Moreover, clinical judgments underlying case conceptualisations are prone to cognitive biases and limited reliability (Lutz et al., 2022; Scholten et al., 2025). Modular treatment frameworks, such as the Unified Protocol for emotional disorders (Barlow et al., 2017), offer an alternative to rigid protocols. Process-based therapy has been proposed as an advancement to evidence-based practice in order to directly address processes of change instead of mere symptoms (Hofmann & Hayes, 2019). However, evidence is not yet sufficient to delineate process-intervention matches.

In parallel, data-informed decision-support systems that integrate clinical expertise into their statistical models have been proposed to address limitations of intuitive clinical judgement (Burger et al., 2022; Levinson et al., 2024).

Across psychotherapy research, support-tools have been developed to match interventions to targets (e.g. Fernandez et al., 2017; Kaiser & Roth, 2022; Rubel et al., 2018).

For mood and anxiety disorders, the algorithm developed by Fernandez and colleagues (2017) demonstrated promising effects (Fisher et al., 2019). However, evidence for the superiority of such algorithms over usual clinical decision-making remains scarce. Crucially, such approaches presuppose clearly specified links between interventions and the psychological processes they are intended to change. In the absence of structured and empirically grounded target-intervention mappings, decision-support systems risk reproducing intuitive or heuristic decision-making rather than improving upon it.

Idiographic and process-focused approaches have been proposed across clinical domains to complement nomothetic models by emphasising within-person change and mechanism-based decision-making (Fisher & Boswell, 2016; Levinson et al., 2024). Such approaches have shown promise in other heterogeneous conditions, including depression (Fisher et al., 2019) and eating disorders (Levinson et al., 2023). Both studies underscore the need for frameworks that systematically link interventions to treatment targets.

Personalisation in chronic pain treatment

In chronic pain research, structured approaches to matching interventions to treatment targets remain particularly underdeveloped (Mauck et al., 2022). Existing personalisation strategies in chronic pain illustrate this limitation in different ways. Stratified care models assign patients to different treatment intensities based on group-level risk profiles (Scholten & Glombiewski, 2024) and have shown modest benefits in low back pain (Foster et al., 2014; Hill et al., 2011). However, recent meta-analytic evidence suggests limited advantages over usual care (Chiodo & Haley, 2024). In addition, stratified approaches do not specify how particular interventions affect individual processes.

More highly personalised treatments for chronic pain, often based on patients' preferences, have also shown encouraging results (Åsenlöf et al., 2005 , 2009; Evers et al., 2002; Ferwerda et al., 2017; Gasslander et al., 2022; Kerns et al., 2014; van Koulil et al., 2010). At the same time, preference-based personalisation remains vulnerable to bias and does not ensure that selected interventions are optimally aligned with the most relevant treatment targets for a given individual. Robust moderators of treatment effects have yet to be identified in chronic pain research (Murillo et al., 2022), while traditional mediation and moderation models may be ill-suited to capture complex, non-linear, and reciprocal processes (Hayes et al., 2019).

Current study

Taken together, this raises several key questions for personalised psychotherapy: In the absence of a comprehensive empirical evidence base, how can personalised treatment decisions be improved? Which psychological processes should be assessed, which interventions are best suited to address them, and how should interventions be systematically matched to treatment targets?

One approach to addressing the gap between intuitive and data-based decision-making is the systematic involvement of clinicians in the development of decision-support tools. In other clinical contexts, expert-informed approaches have been used to formalise interventiontarget relationships and guide treatment selection (Bartels et al., 2022; Burger et al., 2022; Kaiser & Roth, 2022; Mauck et al., 2022). Involving science experts may further help bridge the science-practice gap. The present study therefore aimed to develop a Matching Matrix, that is, a structured framework linking psychological chronic pain-related processes to the two CBT modules expected to target them most effectively, using a group Delphi approach to establish high agreement among experts (Niederberger et al., 2024).

Methods

The study was preregistered (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/MNUQA will be provided after peer-review) and approved by the university's local ethics committee (#LEK-589). Informed consent as well as all data were assessed online using the platform SoSci Survey (Leiner, 2024). Patients as well as the general public have not been involved in the study's conceptualisation. Reporting standards are provided in the Appendix (A) using the DELPHISTAR protocol (Niederberger et al., 2024).

Design

The aim of the present study was to develop a Matching Matrix assigning two CBT modules ("first choice" and "second choice") to 23 treatment targets (i. e. items assessing facets of chronic pain processes, see Study Materials). To bridge the science-practice gap and bring in multiple perspectives, the development process was designed to take place in close collaboration with clinicians as well as science experts. For this purpose, the Delphi technique represents a suitable method.

The Delphi technique is used to survey experts in the field, usually across multiple rounds, in order to facilitate the development of consensus, or at a minimum increase agreement (Boulkedid et al., 2011; Niederberger et al., 2024; Powell, 2003; Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015). However, consensus does not necessarily lead to the best or "correct" results (Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015). Moreover, when consensus develops across repeated rounds, it cannot be ruled out that this reflects normative processes, such as conformity pressure, rather than convergence towards the most well-supported judgment (Powell, 2003).

Consensus has also been criticised as a stopping criterion because it is inconsistently defined and reported across Delphi studies (Diamond et al., 2014).

Against this background, the following approach was implemented in the present study: A group Delphi approach was adopted, whereby separate groups of clinicians were invited to openly discuss and provide anonymous responses to an online survey (Niederberger et al., 2024). Following common recommendations, the number of Delphi rounds was set a priori to two (Diamond et al., 2014; Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015), resulting in Study Phases 1 and 2. In Study Phase 3, a focus group was conducted with science experts to review the results of the Delphi groups. For each phase, a selection criterion was defined a priori. These criteria were intended to identify promising treatment-target matches for further investigation rather than to establish definitive consensus or empirically validated treatment recommendations. The specific criteria are described below along with the associated study phases. Variability in responses was assessed in Phase 1 to characterise the distribution of expert judgments (see Analyses) (Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015). Rather than using consensus as a stopping criterion, agreement was used to operationalise the extent to which a treatment module was consistently recommended for a given psychological process.

Sample

For study phases 1 and 2, clinicians from inpatient and outpatient settings were included. As recommended (Vogt et al., 2004), we aimed to conduct five groups, with an overall target sample size of n = 25. Clinicians were recruited via the university outpatient clinic and local inpatient clinics with dedicated pain treatment units. In inpatient clinics, the whole practitioner team was invited to participate, therefore different professions are represented.

Only participants who agreed to be contacted again in phase 1 were invited to the second Delphi round (phase 2).

For the science expert focus group (phase 3), we aimed for a sample size of n = 5. Science experts were identified through an academic network supported by the Research Foundation -Flanders (FWO, Research Community PAIN). We recruited researchers from this network based on the following two criteria via targeted e-mail invitations: 1) substantial practical and scientific expertise, 2) ensuring representation of different areas of CBT (e.g., third-wave approaches and exposure-based interventions).

Knowledge of CBT interventions and having treated at least one chronic pain patient were defined as inclusion criteria for both science and clinical experts. These criteria allowed the inclusion of different professions and levels of experience, consistent with the recommendation of recruiting heterogeneous samples for Delphi studies to enhance the validity of the results (Baker et al., 2006), whilst ensuring the necessary knowledge to match CBT interventions to specific treatment targets. CBT knowledge was assessed on a 7-point scale (1 = no knowledge,7 = in-depth knowledge). Participants who indicated knowledge below 4 ("basic knowledge") were excluded from analyses.

Since the expertise indicators including the inclusion criteria were assessed anonymously in the online survey, participants were not excluded from participating in the group Delphi procedure, but their data was excluded before analyses. The conducting researcher (first author) did not observe a negative influence of excluded participants on the discussion process.

In Delphi studies, expertise is usually used as an inclusion criterion (Powell, 2003; Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015). However, the concept of expertise remains poorly defined (Baker et al., 2006). Rather than operationalising expertise through predefined eligibility criteria, relevant indicators for clinical and scientific expertise were retrieved from relevant literature (Baker et al., 2006; Hill et al., 2017; Kurniawan et al., 2023; Overholser, 2010), assessed via self-report, and will be reported in detail in the sample description, in accordance with recommendations (Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015). These indicators for example included years of professional experience, number of treated chronic pain patients, or self-ratings of empathic skills for clinicians, and taking part in national and international collaborations and self-rated communication skills for science experts.

Procedure

The complete study procedure is summarised in Figure 1. All assessments took place between January and March 2025.

Phase 1: clinicians first Delphi round

The aim of phase 1 was to develop an initial Matching Matrix based on clinicians' recommendations. As selection criterion, a majority of clinicians (> 50 %) recommending the same module for the same treatment target was set.

Phase 1 represents the first Delphi round and was conducted in separate groups to develop an initial Matching Matrix based on clinicians' recommendations. Discussions were conducted separately in five groups, with each round building iteratively on the previous one.

All groups were conducted and moderated by the first author (first author), a female licensed psychotherapist (CBT) employed at the university as a PhD student. She did not partake in the open discussion, but kept track of time, answered questions regarding targets or modules, and moderated the discussion ensuring that all participants felt comfortable to speak. She also ensured that the discussion remained on the topic and ensured that arguments were not based on misunderstandings or incorrect information. In two groups, participating clinicians worked at the university outpatient clinic, therefore knowing the conducting researcher (first author).

Otherwise there was no personal contact between the conducting researcher and participants prior to or after conduction. Licensed psychotherapists and physicians received continuing education credits for their participation. The discussions were not recorded.

Each group took between 60 and 90 minutes. Face-to-face groups took place in the university outpatient clinic and local inpatient clinics, online groups were conducted via the platform Zoom (https://www.zoom.com/). The format of the groups depended on the capacities of the clinics and the interviewer. Only participating clinicians and the conducting researcher were present during conduction.

All groups followed the same structured procedure: Firstly, informed consent was obtained via an online survey. This survey followed the approach described by Kaiser and Roth (2022) and allowed for anonymous responses. The clinicians were informed regarding the affiliation of the conducting researcher as well as the aim of the study project. Second, sociodemographic data and self-reported expertise indicators were assessed in the online survey. Third, each item of the ProCEss item set, a German item set assessing various psychological processes related to chronic pain (see Study Materials) (references), was presented and the clinicians were asked to select their first and second choice CBT module for each item. The clinicians were instructed to imagine a patient presenting for an initial assessment session whose most promising target process was represented by the item currently displayed. For positively worded items (e. g. self-efficacy), the clinicians were asked to imagine a patient with low scores, with the therapeutic goal being to strengthen this process. This first rating was made anonymously in the survey. Fourth, in the first group, the clinicians were instructed to discuss their selections. From the second group, the two most frequently selected modules per item were presented. The clinicians were invited to provide arguments in favour of as well as against the presented module choices and could suggest and justify other options. Fifth, clinicians provided a second rating that was later used for analyses as it was considered to reflect the more informed decision.

Phase 2: clinicians second Delphi round

The aim of phase 2 was to assess the agreement of the clinicians with the Matching Matrix developed based on phase 1. As selection criterion, a mean agreement of >5 on a 7point scale (0 = do not agree at all,6 = completely agree) for each target-module match was set.

Phase 2 represents the second Delphi round. It was conducted online and could be completed by clinicians over a period of two weeks. Study information was provided in written form with the invitation email as well as in the online survey to download. The clinicians gave their informed consent in the online survey.

After providing sociodemographic and expertise information, the clinicians were presented with the results of phase 1 one match at a time. If the same module had been selected most frequently as both first and second choice, the next most frequently selected module was presented as the second option. In the event of a tie between modules for either the first or second choice, all tied modules were displayed, and participants were asked to rank them. They also had the option to provide written comments. These qualitative comments were used in cases that did not meet the pre-defined selection criteria to complete the matching matrix.

Phase 3: science expert focus group

The aim of phase 3 was to review the clinicians' selections by a focus group with psychological science experts. The primary criterion for final module selection in this group was majority agreement (> 50%) for each target-module match. If no clear majority emerged for a given target in Phase 1, the decision could be overruled by the focus group of science experts. That means, a module was considered accepted if a majority was reached either among the clinicians or among the science experts, or among both. Since the science experts were not participating in the previous phases, this phase was not considered another Delphi round. This rationale provided clear decision rules in the case of unfulfilled majority criteria in Phases 1 and 3.

Study information was provided in written form via email prior to the session. All science experts gave verbal consent to the recording of the discussion.

The science experts received the same theoretical introduction as the clinicians in phase 1. Recording began after this introduction, when the science experts were presented with the results of the clinicians' ratings of phase 1. They were invited to discuss potential contraindications for the selected modules and to specify under which conditions the secondchoice module might be preferable to the first-choice module. The recorded discussion was transcribed by a research assistant also present in the meeting for qualitative assessment of the discussion. The transcript was not returned to the participants. The qualitative comments transcribed were used in cases that did not meet the pre-defined selection criteria to complete the matching matrix.

Following the discussion of each target-module match, science experts completed an online survey in which they indicated their agreement with each target-module match on a dichotomous scale (agreement vs. disagreement), regardless of the position of the module as first or second choice. They also provided sociodemographic and self-assessed expertise indicators (see Study Materials). The science experts' focus group took 90 minutes. Note. Solid frame = face-to-face, dashed frame = online; each group in phase 1 was presented cumulative results of all previous groups; this figure was created using Microsoft PowerPoint

Study Materials

Treatment Targets

The set of potential targets was based on the German "Prozesse Chronischer Schmerzen ErfaSSen" (ProCEss; English: "Assessing chronic pain processes") item set.

Within this item set, psychological processes were selected based on established psychological models of chronic pain (e.g. the Fear-Avoidance model ( Vlaeyen et al., 2016))as well as the IMMPACT recommendations of important pain experience variables (Dworkin et al., 2005). The ProCEss item set is theory-driven, based on psychological models of chronic pain, and has been qualitatively validated in German language (Reference) and demonstrates overall sufficient psychometric properties in the German version (Reference).

Of the ProCEss item set, 23 items assessing specific manifestations of the processes catastrophising, avoidance behaviour, depressive symptoms, acceptance, values-based action, expectations, thought suppression, task persistency, positive affect, negative affect, selfefficacy, and self-compassion, were used in this study (for items, also see Table 2). The original German version of the ProCEss item set as well as relevant evaluative data can be found on the ProCEss repository (link will be provided after peer-review to retain anonymity). B).

CBT Modules

The treatment modules were selected to represent conceptually distinct strategies that could be evaluated individually within the matching framework. Consequently, interventions that were considered to reflect overarching therapeutic skills, e.g. mindfulness, were not included as separate modules, as they are considered to be embedded within several modules, e.g. attention regulation and acceptance-based interventions.

Analysis

All analyses were carried out using R Studio (R version 4.4.1) (Posit Team, 2024), using the following packages: dplyr (Wickham et al., 2023), forcats (Wickham & RStudio, 2023a), ggplot2 (Wickham, Chang, et al., 2025), openxlsx (Schauberger et al., 2025), stringr (Wickham, Posit Software, et al., 2025), tidyr (Wickham et al., 2024), tidyverse (Wickham & RStudio, 2023b), and writexl (Ooms & McNamara, 2025). ChatGPT (artificial intelligence) was used for generating R code and for correcting errors in the script.

The majority of clinicians recommending the same module (selection criterion of phase 1) was calculated as frequencies with which each module was recommended per target after group discussion.

As preregistered, the Gibbs-Martin Index was calculated to quantify variability in clinicians' selections (Gibbs & Martin, 1962). Given that participants could choose from nine predefined CBT modules, the index could range from 0 to 0.89. The closer the index is to 0, the fewer categories are selected -indicating a clearer consensus. Conversely, values approaching the upper limit suggest more evenly distributed selections across modules, reflecting lower agreement. The index was calculated across all item-module matches for the first and second rating and separately for the first and second choices, resulting in four indices (first rating -first choices, first rating -second choices, second rating -first choices, second rating -second choices).

Qualitative comments of phases 2 and 3 were only used if the predefined selection criteria were not met. If necessary, the qualitative comments were reviewed by the study team. The study team consisted of three female psychologists, one licensed psychotherapist and PhD (co-author), one licensed psychotherapist and PhD student (first author), and one psychotherapist in training and PhD student. Qualitative comments were reviewed descriptively rather than analysed using a formal qualitative methodology. Their purpose was to identify alternative module recommendations and to better understand reasons underlying disagreement with the proposed recommendations from phase 1. Information retrieved from the qualitative comments complemented the recommendation frequencies of phase 1 that were also reviewed in cases of unmet selection criteria.

Results

Samples

In the first Delphi round (phase 1), n = 25 clinicians participated in five focus groups.

Three clinicians were excluded from the final analyses: two participants reported no prior treatment experience with chronic pain patients, and one rated their CBT knowledge below "basic knowledge". This resulted in a final sample size of n = 22.

The sociodemographic and expertise characteristics of all three samples are summarised in Table 1. A more detailed overview of those variables is provided in the Appendix (C1). 23 clinicians were contacted via e-mail to participate in phase 2.16 of them (69.57 %) completed the online survey for the second round. One participant was excluded due to insufficient CBT knowledge, resulting in a final sample-size of n = 15. Reasons for not participating in this phase are not known. A more detailed overview of the sociodemographic and expertise information is provided in the Appendix (C2). The sample was compared to the sample of phase 1 with regard to all expertise indicators, as well as age, gender, secondary school qualification, and professional affiliation. No significant differences were found between the two samples on any of these variables.

Four out of the five contacted pain science experts participated in the online focus group. Results of phase 1: clinicians first Delphi round

For the first 23 first-choice selections, 66.40 % of recommendations met the criterion of a simple majority. In three cases, exactly 50 % of clinicians selected the same module as their first choice. Only for one target did the first-choice module fall short of a simple majority, with 45.46 %.

Regarding the second-choice selections, the criterion of a simple majority was met for 46.84 % of the 23 targets. Agreement in percent for both the second as well as the first rating and majority outcomes for both the first and second ratings are provided online on OSF (link will be provided after peer-review to retain anonymity).

In all four instances (first rating -first choice, first rating -second choice, second rating -first choice, second rating -second choice), the Gibbs-Martin Index was 0.5, indicating a moderate consensus among clinicians across items, with some preference patterns emerging alongside notable distributional spread. Accordingly, no differences from the first to the second rating and between first and second choices in the variability of clinicians' recommendations could be detected.

Results of phase 2: clinicians second Delphi round

Regarding the mean agreement rating of > 5 on a 7-point scale, all first-choice modules met this threshold. Among the second-choice modules, three did not meet this selection criterion. A detailed breakdown of all agreement scores as well as the ranking of unclear choices is provided online (link will be provided after peer-review to retain anonymity).

Results of phase 3: science expert focus group

Regarding the primary criterion of this focus group -namely, a majority agreement (i. e. > 2) -the criterion was met for 31 out of 46 target-module matches (67.40 %). 22 targetmodule matches received unanimous agreement from all science experts.

Explorative Results

Frequency of module choices

Figure 2 illustrates the frequency with which the nine CBT modules were selected as first or second choices in the clinicians' rating after discussion in phase 1. It is noteworthy that "third-wave" modules such as Self-Compassion, Acceptance, and Values were selected considerably more frequently than "classical" CBT modules like Attentional Control or Relaxation. This trend was also explicitly noted by several clinicians, who reported choosing "third-wave" modules more frequently in the study context than they typically do in routine clinical practice, where Attentional Control and Relaxation are more commonly applied.

Notably, all nine modules were selected at least once, suggesting the overall clinical relevance and perceived applicability of the pre-selected module pool. Note. Red bars = first choice, blue bars = second choice. Bars represent the absolute number with which the modules were selected as first or second choice across all targets by all clinical experts (22 experts recommended 23 first and second choices each, resulting in 506 first and 506 second choices). This figure was created in R Studio.

Agreement shift from first to second rating

Another noteworthy observation concerns changes in agreement in the clinicians' recommendations before and after the discussion in phase 1. These two ratings can themselves be interpreted as separate rounds, with the second rating reflecting a more informed decision following group discussion. For the first-choice modules, agreement increased in 18 instances and remained unchanged in two. In three instances, agreement decreased from the first to the second rating. Overall, the agreement regarding the first-choice modules increased from 56.72 % before to 66.40 % after discussion.

For the second-choice modules, agreement increased after group discussion for 18 targets and remained unchanged in three instances. In two instances, agreement decreased from the first to the second rating. Overall, agreement regarding the second-choice modules increased from 38.34 % before to 46.84 % after group discussion. Agreement percentages from the first and second rating are provided online (link will be provided after peer-review to retain anonymity).

Data saturation

In qualitative research, anticipating the point of data saturation is crucial for planning the number of rounds, focus groups, and overall sample size. In this study, module choices were descriptively summarised based on the most frequently selected options after each group of phase 1 (link will be provided after peer-review to retain anonymity). For eight out of 23 items, both the first-and second-choice modules were already clearly established following the first focus group. For an additional five targets, the first-choice module (but not the second-choice) was determined after the first group. Only one item showed a change after the fifth focus group, resulting in a tie. Overall, this descriptive analysis suggests that for the majority of items, module preferences were established within the first one to three focus group sessions, with only minor changes occurring during the final two groups.

Overall results

The final Matching Matrix is presented in Table 2. Of all 46 target-module matches, 21 (46.65 %) fulfilled all three primary criteria: a majority of clinicians in phase 1, a mean agreement of > 5 in phase 2, and a majority of science experts in phase 3. For an additional 17 matches (36.96 %), at least one majority -either among clinicians or science experts -was present, and these matches were therefore also included in the final matrix. Of these 17 matches, there were two that were included despite missing two criteria. The remaining eight target-module matches (17.39 %), all of which involved second-choice modules, were subject to discussion within the study team. These were selected based on the frequency of module selections in phase 1 and the qualitative comments from both phases 2 and 3. A detailed summary of the final Matching Matrix, including the fulfilment of each phase criterion and the rationale for decision on the eight discussed items is provided in the Appendix (D).

Discussion

The aim of this mixed-methods study was to develop a structured Matching Matrix linking two CBT modules to individual, chronic pain-related processes, thereby addressing a central challenge in personalised psychotherapy: how to support clinical decision-making in the absence of robust, component-level empirical data. Using a group Delphi approach with clinicians and a focus group with science experts, a complete matrix covering 23 target processes was generated. Notably, first-choice module selections showed high robustness, as all first-choice selections met the predefined criteria and required no further discussion by the study team. This suggests that clinicians and science experts share a substantial degree of implicit agreement regarding core intervention-target relationships in chronic pain treatment.

On the other hand, there were two module recommendations included in the final Matching Matrix that missed two of the three predefined criteria, and no recommendation reached unanimous agreement, potentially reflecting remaining discrepancies in the experts' clinical reasoning.

Eight of the 23 second-choice modules required additional discussion within the study team, as they did not meet the obligatory criteria. This may reflect the broader framing of second-choice modules as "alternatives", potentially encouraging clinicians to consider a wider range of options and thereby reducing consensus. These findings support the idea that there may be multiple viable intervention strategies for addressing a given target process (Scheidegger et al., 2023), reinforcing the idea that personalised treatment should accommodate flexibility rather than enforce singular solutions.

Across both science experts and clinician groups, "third-wave" CBT modules (e. g.

Self-Compassion, Acceptance) were more frequently selected and received higher agreement.

This may reflect their perceived relevance for chronic pain, where acceptance-based and contextual approaches are widely regarded as particularly suitable. At the same time, this tendency could reflect cognitive biases -such as availability or recency effects due to recent training experiences. Conformity effects seem unlikely to have primarily contributed to the preferential selection of third-wave modules, as these modules were also selected most frequently by clinicians in the initial independent rating in Phase 1 (see Appendix E). In the case of science experts, this may in part be explained by selection bias, as two of the four participants reported specific expertise in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy.

Overall, our findings cannot determine whether the greater emphasis on third-wave modules reflects a bias in expert judgment or the composition of the sample or a genuine perception that these modules are particularly relevant for the psychological processes assessed. The present design was not intended to distinguish between these explanations. A more systematic documentation of the arguments underlying module selection would have allowed for a deeper examination of these influences and represents an important direction for future research. Additionally, investigating possible differences in clinical decision-making between therapists in training and licensed psychotherapists or even between male and female clinicians presents another step for future research. In conclusion, replication with larger and more representative samples of clinicians (e.g. from community-based settings) and researchers could help determine the robustness of the pattern found in this study and clarify the extent to which it reflects expertise, sample composition, or systematic biases in treatment recommendations.

Interestingly, various modules were selected for items of the same process. This observation supports the notion that discernible facets of the same process may require different treatment approaches, and that using for example sum scores of processes assessed with multiple items might result in loss of therapy-relevant information (Pena Loray et al., 2025). More broadly, these results echo ongoing debates regarding mechanisms of change in psychotherapy. A central assumption underlying the present Matching Matrix, as well as previous attempts to develop matching matrices or algorithmic decision-tools (cf. Fernandez et al., 2017), is that a given intervention can be matched to a specific treatment target.

However, it seems unlikely that specific interventions only affect one target at a time (Eronen, 2020; Henry et al., 2022), just as different treatment modules may influence the same target or outcome (Scheidegger et al., 2023). This is consistent with research comparing different treatment approaches (e.g., Zgierska et al., 2025), as well as with the present finding that clinical experts did not consistently recommend the same two modules for a given target.

Moreover, emerging evidence questions the existence of strictly intervention-specific mechanisms (Burns, 2025), suggesting that selecting modules for isolated targets may be overly simplistic.

Nevertheless, identifying a primary treatment target may remain clinically useful. In practice, selecting an intervention based on the process facet considered most relevant to a patient's current difficulties provides a feasible starting point for treatment planning, even if or even because the selected intervention is likely to affect additional process facets.

Understanding the differential effects of theoretically distinct interventions thus remains a key challenge for improving CBT (Cohen et al., 2023).

Accounting systematically for interconnected effects would require moving beyond a one-to-one matching approach. Future work may therefore benefit from identifying efficacy profiles that capture patterns of effects across multiple interacting targets. Such analyses may become increasingly feasible as larger datasets linking interventions, psychological processes, and treatment outcomes become available. Until then, expert-based matching provides a pragmatic approach to structuring clinical decision-making in the absence of sufficient empirical data.

At the same time, identified moderators are likely unspecific to the treatment form (Chen et al., 2023). Accordingly, the treatment strategy might be less relevant for the outcome than nonspecific treatment mechanisms, highlighting the need to investigate both intervention-specific and common mechanisms in personalised CBT.

Data saturation within the clinician sample may have been reached prior to the fifth clinician group. From a resource-oriented perspective, fewer groups could therefore be sufficient for developing a Matching Matrix of this kind. The focus group of science experts proved to be useful for validating the clinicians' selections, with 17 of the final target-module matches being supported by at least one majority criterion.

In most cases, agreement between clinicians in phase 1 increased from first to second rating. This might reflect a tendency to agree with the previous focus group, the results of which were presented after the first rating, enhanced by the prompt to deliver arguments in favour with these recommendations. Cases in which agreement decreased could be explained by especially empathetically made arguments against the previous results that did not occur very often. The fact that agreement also decreased in some instances implicates that clinicians did not uniformly adopt the recommendations of previous groups or of one another. However, these explanations are based on the impression of the conducting researcher (first author) and cannot definitely be determined due to the lack of recordings of Phase 1. Future research should consider transcribing the arguments provided so that agreement shifts can be analysed more systematically.

From a clinical perspective, personalised psychotherapy rarely involves a single intervention in isolation. Rather, treatment decisions unfold iteratively, requiring clinicians to determine not only which, but also when to apply an intervention (Fisher & Boswell, 2016).

Strengths and Limitations

This study adhered to current recommendations for systematic and structured clinician surveys (Kaiser & Roth, 2022), employing a collaborative framework to enhance the acceptability of the resulting matrix (Levinson et al., 2024) as well as its ecological validity, and predefining methodological procedures in accordance with established guidelines (Diamond et al., 2014; Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015). In response to common criticisms of Delphi studies, indicators of clinical expertise were assessed following relevant recommendations (Baker et al., 2006; Boulkedid et al., 2011; Hill et al., 2017; Overholser, 2010) and transparently reported alongside consensus in the form of percentage agreement (Diamond et al., 2014).

A further strength of the present study lies in the composition of the expert samples.

The literature recommends heterogenous samples involving experts from diverse professional backgrounds and settings (J. Baker et al., 2006). Furthermore, such an approach reflects the multimodal treatment reality of chronic pain. In this study, a minimum level of expertise was ensured, while still allowing for a broad range of professional roles and clinical experience.

As such, we consider the clinician sample to be well suited to the study objective, with the results likely to be both ecologically valid and reasonably reliable. The inclusion of psychological science experts complemented the clinician perspective by introducing a more theoretical and research-informed viewpoint. Taken together, these two expert groups may contribute to bridging the science-practice gap -an effect that could be amplified by bringing science experts and clinicians into direct discussion. Additionally, both the number of focus groups (Vogt et al., 2004) and the sample sizes in the Delphi rounds (J. Baker et al., 2006) followed established methodological recommendations.

From an epistemic perspective, the present study should be understood as an interim step between intuitive clinical judgement and fully data-driven decision-support systems. It reflects clinician and researcher recommendations in the sense of a hypothesis-generating framework warranting empirical evaluation. While previous research suggests a likely mismatch between clinical judgement and data-oriented decision-making tools (Fernandez et al., 2017), collaboration with clinicians appears to be a necessary interim step to generate robust data for algorithmic approaches. The method used to create the present Matching Matrix is replicable, and applying the Matching Matrix in psychotherapy research will allow studying module-specific effects on clearly defined treatment targets.

However, patients have not been included in this study project, which should be considered in future studies. It is yet unclear how algorithmic decision guidelines such as this Matching Matrix can be incorporated in an interactive, shared-decision making process (Wester et al., 2025), that is and should be the gold-standard in clinical practice. Especially as long as evidence for algorithmic decision-tools is scarce, additional information such as patients' preferences should be included (Wester et al., 2025). In this study, such additional information was considered regarding contraindications for certain interventions and were discussed in the researcher focus group. We advise users of the Matching Matrix to reflect if any adverse effects are anticipated when following the recommendations for any individual patient, and of course to obtain informed consent.

The use of a predefined pool of CBT modules introduced a top-down element to the procedure, potentially omitting relevant interventions (e. g. problem-solving). The same holds true for the predefined set of process items. However, earlier, unpublished study projects had shown that, in the absence of a predefined module pool, discussions became overly broad and unmanageable within the given timeframe. Future research should review and extend the predefined pool of CBT modules with other important treatment strategies for chronic pain such as sleep hygiene, problem solving, or communication skills. It should also consider further strategies to select treatment targets, for example Perceived Causal Networks (Klintwall et al., 2021; Vogel et al., 2025) Additionally, the limit of two modules per target was chosen given the timely constraints of the selection process and with the goal of providing a concise recommendation for clinical practice. Alternative to selecting only two treatment modules per target, all predefined modules could be ranked for each given target, resulting in a priority evaluation for each target-module match.

Some clinicians reported potential framing effects or the tendency to project personal clinical experience onto the items, since they were presented without contextual case vignettes. One promising alternative to mitigate this limitation could be to reverse the selection logic -asking clinicians to identify the most relevant target processes for specific modules, rather than selecting modules for processes. Another possibility would be the use of personas to guide the discussion process (Bartels et al., 2023). Such personas or case vignettes could also account for different contexts, goals, individual illness beliefs, and also comorbidities and according treatments.

From a methodological perspective, potential order effects cannot be ruled out, as randomisation of item presentation was not feasible. Future studies should consider randomising the order of items or modules. Moreover, due to time limitations, the discussions among clinicians and science experts were relatively brief and should be regarded as thought prompts rather than in-depth deliberations.

The sequential design of Phase 1 may have introduced conformity effects and reduced the independence of recommendations. However, these effects were likely limited due to the independent, anonymous first rating and explicit encouragements to discuss arguments against the emerging group recommendation prior to the second rating. The results indicated decreasing agreement from the first to the second rating in few instances, suggesting that recommendations were not uniformly influenced by preceding group decisions. Future research could investigate differences between first and second ratings more systematically, including whether such changes are associated with differential treatment effectiveness.

Recent methodological recommendations for Delphi studies commonly suggest conducting three rounds and using a consensus threshold of at least 80 % in the final round (Hohmann et al., 2025). In the present study, the number of rounds was a prior limited to two, and the agreement thresholds applied in Phases 1 and 3 were below this recommended level.

Given the hypothesis-generating aim of this study, the heterogeneous composition of the clinician sample, and the fact that three complementary selection criteria were applied across the different phases, the liberal agreement thresholds appear justified and still allow to build upon the results for future research. Nevertheless, future research should consider replicating the present findings using a third Delphi round and more stringent consensus criteria to examine the stability and robustness of the identified matches.

Since no transcripts of the focus groups in phase 1 were made, more detailed insights regarding agreement and disagreement of the clinicians cannot be reported. The option to leave comments in phase 2 was used by few clinicians as well. Future research should incorporate a more systematic assessment and analysis of qualitative data.

Additionally, allowing more extensive discussions in future work may facilitate clearer consensus-building and potentially lead to greater convergence among participants.

Conclusion

In the present study, a mixed methods approach including Delphi technique and focus groups was applied in close collaboration with practicing clinicians as well as renowned pain science experts that resulted in a matrix linking CBT modules of first and second choice to 23 chronic pain processes. By formalising intervention-target relationships, the present Matching Matrix addresses a central bottleneck in personalised psychotherapy: the absence of structured guidance when empirical evidence is incomplete. The procedure used to develop this Matching Matrix is replicable, suitable to bridge the science-practice gap, and can guide future efforts to personalise psychotherapy, also beyond the context of chronic pain.

Several key questions remain to be answered, including which processes are most suitable as therapeutic targets, how they can best be assessed, and which interventions are most effective in addressing them. Ultimately, the aim of research in this area should not be to replace clinicians, but to support them in making evidence-based, personalised decisions (Levinson et al., 2024; Lutz et al., 2022; Wester et al., 2025). The present study may serve as an interim step towards a more data-based clinical decision process. A stronger empirical basis is urgently needed to predict the effects of particular methods on defined target processes (Cohen et al., 2023; Murillo et al., 2022) and to determine the usefulness of specific targets versus more complex efficacy profiles in the absence of intervention-specific mechanisms of action (Burns, 2025).

Fig 2

Fig.2Overall frequency of module choices across all targets and clinical experts

Although the present Matching Matrix does not prescribe a fixed intervention sequence, it is compatible with such an iterative approach by supporting repeated target selection and module assignment across treatment phases. Future research should examine how such matrices can be integrated into longitudinal treatment planning, including the determination of meaningful endpoints of the intervention and the treatment in general. In clinical practice, application of this matching matrix would encompass identifying a treatment target, e.g. using the ProCEss item set (V. E.Hofmann, Glombiewski, Heider, et al., 2026a; V. E. Hofmann, Glombiewski, Prasch, et al., 2026), and using the Matching Matrix as guidance for treatment mapping. However, since the actual efficacy of the Matching Matrix has not yet been evaluated, we do not recommend relying on the Matching Matrix alone in routine clinical practice.While the present matrix does not replace empirical effect estimates, it provides a formalised representation of expert knowledge that can serve as a foundation for future datadriven refinement. Importantly, the challenge of evidence-based personalisation in the absence of sufficient empirical data is not unique to chronic pain, but reflects a broader issue in psychotherapy research, where the aspiration for personalised treatment often outpaces the available evidence base. Consequently, both the Matching Matrix itself as well as the detailed description of the development process present valuable starting points for future research on personalised CBT within and beyond the context of chronic pain. With growing evidence on the effects of specific interventions, clinical decision-support tools may become increasingly data-driven, complementing rather than replacing clinical judgement. Advances in artificial intelligence may further enhance such tools by facilitating the integration of complex evidence into treatment recommendations or identifying efficacy profiles beyond simple intervention-target matches. Such tools might also include whether patients receive multiple (multimodal) treatments, possibly in different settings by different practitioners, at the same time and how they can best be coordinated.

Future

research can build on this Matching Matrix to investigate the effects of individualised intervention selection and to further evaluate whether process-based matching improves treatment outcomes. Moreover, the procedure described in this study may provide a framework for developing personalised treatment recommendations in other areas where empirical evidence for specific treatments is currently limited. Until sufficient data is available to support data-driven algorithms, larger samples of clinical and scientific experts may further strengthen the robustness of the Matching Matrix and enable subgroup analyses. Such analyses could provide further insights into clinical reasoning across different professional backgrounds and levels of expertise.
